title: Naomi Watts to Receive Zurich Film Festival’s Golden Eye Award for ‘The Housewife’
description:
Zurich Film Festival is to honor actress Naomi Watts with the Golden Eye Award for her performance in Ben Shirinian’s “The Housewife.”

	In Zurich,
body:
Zurich Film Festival is to honor actress Naomi Watts with the Golden Eye Award for her performance in Ben Shirinian’s “The Housewife.”

	In Zurich, she will present the film, in which she portrays the enigmatic wife of a suspected Nazi. The actress will personally accept the award on Sept. 26 and offer insights into her career during a ZFF Masters session.

	The festival described Watts, who has earned two Academy Award nominations, as “an artist renowned for her emotional depth, versatility and unwavering commitment to her roles.”
	

	In “The Housewife,” she plays an elegant and inscrutable woman living in 1960s New York whose flawless façade gradually begins to crack when a young journalist from the New York Times uncovers clues about her husband’s dark past.


	Christian Jungen, CEO of the festival, said, “Since her breakthrough in David Lynch’s ‘Mulholland Drive,’ Naomi Watts has been one of the most fascinating actresses of our time. Her greatest performances thrive on the tension between glamour and darkness, between what a character reveals and what she conceals – making her the kind of character actress Hitchcock would have loved.

	“In ‘The Housewife,’ she masters this ambiguity as an elegant and mysterious woman. At the same time, the film tells a true story that powerfully illustrates how indispensable investigative journalism is in uncovering historical crimes. Naomi Watts delivers one of the most compelling performances of her career.”

	Watts said, “It is such an honor to be presented with the Golden Eye Award from Zurich Film Festival. I cannot wait to be there, accepting this award among such great company, and I thank the film festival for honoring my role in this film.”

schema.headline: Naomi Watts to Receive Zurich Film Festival’s Golden Eye Award for ‘The Housewife’

title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Moving Back to U.K. in Shock Decision
description: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are moving back to the U.K. with their children after living in California for the past six years, according to Peopl
body:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are moving back to the U.K. with their children after living in California for the past six years, according to People. The transition back to Britain, which the outlet says will last for “an extended period,” is set to begin in the coming weeks. 

	The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will maintain their home in Montecito, Calif., and the location of their new home is currently unknown, People reports. 


	Harry and Meghan have no imminent plans to relocate or disband their content shop, Archewell Productions, an insider close to the couple said. Same goes for As Ever, Meghan’s consumer lifestyle brand.
	

	King Charles was told Sunday that the Sussexes would be shipping back to the U.K., The New York Times reports. The Times also said that Harry and Meghan will remain non-working royals after their move. 

	The royal couple has seen plenty of ups and downs during their time in the U.S., especially surrounding their Hollywood banner, Archewell Productions, which has struggled to deliver on its goal of creating scripted and nonscripted films and series for all ages. Archewell was launched in 2020 and now mostly platforms Meghan’s As Ever brand. 

	Netflix became one of Archewell’s first major partners in 2020, but the relationship has been strained after six years of low productivity. “The mood in the building is ‘We’re done,’” one Netflix insider told Variety for a cover story about Archewell’s deal with the streamer.

	The pact remains intact for now. In March, Variety reported that Harry and Meghan are developing a film adaptation of the Afghan war memoir, “No Way Out: The Searing True Story of Men Under Siege,” for Netflix. The book tells of British Major Adam Jowett’s command of Easy Company, a unit of Paras and Royal Irish Rangers tasked with protecting the District Centre of Musa Qala in Afghanistan in 2006.

schema.headline: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Moving Back to U.K. in Shock Decision

title: Hayden Panettiere’s Death: DEA Joins Investigation
description:
The Drug Enforcement Administration has joined the investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death, according to ABC News.

	The DEA is entering a join
body:
The Drug Enforcement Administration has joined the investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death, according to ABC News.

	The DEA is entering a joint effort with South Carolina’s Greenville Police Department and the local coroner’s office, according to TMZ.

	Panettiere died Sunday night at age 36. The official cause of death has not yet been determined. In her 2026 memoir “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” Panettiere went into detail about her years-long struggles with drug and alcohol addiction.
	

	After news broke of Panettiere’s death, tributes from across Hollywood came pouring in online. On Wednesday, Jack Coleman, who played her father on “Heroes,” shared an emotional tribute on Instagram.

	“I’m heartbroken. I couldn’t begin to put my thoughts into words until now, and they will be inadequate,” Coleman wrote. “I’ve loved Hayden since day one of the pilot of ‘Heroes,’ 20 years ago, when she introduced herself by shouting ‘daddy’ and throwing her arms around me. From that day on, she called me daddio. She was Haydini, because she was a magician.”

	Christy Carlson Romano, the Disney Channel star who played Ren Stevens on “Even Stevens” and voiced the titular teen spy on “Kim Possible,” likewise shared a remembrance for Panettiere on Wednesday. In an essay for Elle, she compared the trauma of childhood fame to Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE), a brain disease caused by repeated hits to the head.

	“The former child actor exists in a category the world does not know how to hold,” she wrote. “We are children when the public wants to feel protective of us, professionals when the industry wants to profit from us, and spoiled celebrities when we eventually show symptoms of having been both… Early fame is like CTE. Not as a diagnosis. As a way of thinking about repeated impact. We now have language for youth sports: protocols, helmets, parents worried about concussions. But we have almost no language for what happens when stress, scrutiny, rejection, adult pressure, and the collapse of privacy become the architecture of a childhood.”

schema.headline: Hayden Panettiere’s Death: DEA Joins Investigation

title: Ariana Grande Granted Permission to Issue Expedited Subpoenas to Reveal Hacker Identities
description: Ariana Grande has been granted permission to subpoena information that will help reveal the identities of anonymous hackers who allegedly leaked unr
body:
Ariana Grande has been granted permission to subpoena information that will help reveal the identities of anonymous hackers who allegedly leaked unreleased songs and footage from recording sessions and music videos.

	A Los Angeles judge approved Grande’s proposed order for expedited discovery on Tuesday, explaining that because she is unable to identify the hackers, a waiting period should be waived. “Given that there is no one to whom notice can be given anyway, it makes little sense to wait the 16 days,” wrote Judge Mark H. Epstein. “And on the merits of the motion, good cause is shown.”
	

	On Tuesday, attorneys for Grande filed the ex parte application for expedited discovery, arguing that by being unable to name the defendants, the “hacking, theft, dissemination, sales, and publication” of Grande’s creative properties will continue and that there is an “increased risk that additional content will be stolen or sold, and that the account, subscriber, and login data needed to identify Defendants will be lost.”


	Grande initially filed her lawsuit on July 27, targeting a group of unnamed John Does for phishing scams and hacking schemes that have caused “unlawful and egregious theft, dissemination, and exploitation of unreleased content.” Her legal team outlined a pattern of illegal behaviors that targeted the personal digital accounts of photographers and producers who worked closely with her and sold the data and content for “significant sums of money.”

	The suit alleged that hundreds of leaks have occurred over the past decade-and-a-half, noting that in 2023 alone, hackers obtained access to 45 of her unreleased songs and leaked them.

schema.headline: Ariana Grande Granted Permission to Issue Expedited Subpoenas to Reveal Hacker Identities

title: Dane Cook’s Brother Stole $12 Million From Comedian, Hid Bricks of Cash in Pasta Sauce
description:
Uh oh, Spaghetti O’s!

	Dane Cook‘s brother stole $12 million from the comedian and hid bricks of cash inside pasta sauce, a new documentary reveals
body:
Uh oh, Spaghetti O’s!

	Dane Cook‘s brother stole $12 million from the comedian and hid bricks of cash inside pasta sauce, a new documentary reveals.

	Premiering on Sept. 29, “Funny Money: The Dane Cook Story” delves into the financial drama that absorbed the blockbuster comedian in 2008, when his half-brother and business manager, Darryl McCauley, was charged with embezzling at least $12 million from Cook.


	McCauley pleaded guilty to larceny, embezzlement and other charges (along with his wife, Erika) and was ordered to pay back the $12 million. He served a six-year prison sentence and then disappeared entirely. “Where is he? What has he done? How does this end?” Cook narrates in the documentary trailer.
	

	In “Funny Money,” Cook says growing up, he and McCauley both wanted to be stand-up comedians. McCauley ultimately became a corrections officer, while Cook went on to become one of the most commercially successful comics of the 2000s. Cook describes McCauley in the documentary as “a person who spent so much time pretending to be something he wasn’t.”

	Working as the handler of his finances, McCauley began withdrawing sums of $20,000, $50,000 and even $100,000 from Cook’s accounts without him noticing. “I was starting to feel something that I couldn’t really identify,” Cook admits in the trailer. “Was he hiding it in different places, stockpiling this money?”

	Finally, it was revealed that McCauley had stolen a massive amount of money from his famous brother, hiding piles of cash in a safe and even wrapping it in plastic before stashing it inside pasta sauce containers — a storyline straight out of “The Bear.”
	

	While an investigation determined that McCauley had embezzled at least $12 million, Cook believes the amount could be even higher. “I do believe that there’s money out there,” he says in the trailer. “I believe there’s people that know more.”

	“Funny Money: The Dane Cook Story” will be available to stream on demand beginning Sept. 29.

schema.headline: Dane Cook’s Brother Stole $12 Million From Comedian, Hid Bricks of Cash in Pasta Sauce

title: Hayden Panettiere’s ‘Heroes’ Dad Calls Out ‘Predatory’ Paparazzi Who ‘Hunted’ Her and the Press Who Asked ‘Misogynistic’ Questions When She Was a Teen
description: Jack Coleman, the “Heroes” actor who played the father of Hayden Panettiere‘s Claire Bennet, posted an emotional tribute to his late co-star followi
body:
Jack Coleman, the “Heroes” actor who played the father of Hayden Panettiere‘s Claire Bennet, posted an emotional tribute to his late co-star following her death this week at 36 years old. 

	“I’m heartbroken. I couldn’t begin to put my thoughts into words until now, and they will be inadequate,” Coleman wrote on Instagram alongside a carousel of photos of the two actors on the “Heroes” set throughout the years. “I’ve loved Hayden since day one of the pilot of ‘Heroes,’ 20 years ago, when she introduced herself by shouting ‘daddy’ and throwing her arms around me. From that day on, she called me daddio. She was Haydini, because she was a magician.”
	

	Coleman used his tribute to express some of the ways he saw the industry negatively impact his younger co-star, including reporters who would ask her inappropriate questions when she was just a teenager.


	“By 17 she was #1 on IMDB Pro. She was routinely asked obnoxious questions, mostly some version of ‘when are you going to go off the rails?'” Coleman recalled. “Today, we’d recognize those questions for the misogynistic provocations they were.”

	“She was hunted. Everywhere she went, there were photographers with 300 millimeter lenses — the kind that can make even the most innocent activity look sinister,” he continued. “Once, when she came to our house, paparazzi hid in the bushes behind our yard and drove onto neighbors’ lawns. They were predatory. No one, especially a teenager, should be targeted that way.”

	Coleman concluded, “Today I’m filled with sorrow and regret. And anger. But that’s for another time. Right now I want to remember an extraordinary young woman who was blessed and cursed. She was vulnerable. She felt everything. It made her a remarkable actor and susceptible to the heartache and thousand natural shocks that flesh is heir to.”
	

	Coleman and Panettiere played central characters on “Heroes” during its original four season run on NBC from 2006 to 2010. Coleman returned for the 2015 “Reborn” miniseries. Many of Panettiere’s “Heroes” co-stars have posted tributes to her in the wake of her death. Sendhil Ramamurthy, who played Mohinder Suresh, remembered how Panettiere would stand up for mistreated background actors on set and knew every crew member’s name, for instance.

	In an exclusive essay for Variety, “Heroes” creator Tim Kring praised Panettiere as a “singularly talented” actor, adding: “Hayden was a true team player, which was important for a show with a large ensemble cast. She was levelheaded beyond her years as a person, with an almost savant-like quality about her work. It wasn’t just that Hayden could learn lines with ease — it was her rare ability to find and explore the nuances of drama and humor and pathos in any scene she was in.”

	Panettiere’s death is currently under investigation, but there were “not any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances,” according to police.

schema.headline: Hayden Panettiere’s ‘Heroes’ Dad Calls Out ‘Predatory’ Paparazzi Who ‘Hunted’ Her and the Press Who Asked ‘Misogynistic’ Questions When She Was a Teen

title: ‘Lucky’ Creators on Deciding Who Dies in the Finale, Why the Show Really Is Over and Not Knowing About Drew Starkey’s ‘Avid’ Fandom ‘Until We Killed Him’
description:
Aug 19, 2026 4:00pm PT	
	

	
		‘Lucky’ Creators on Deciding Who Dies in the Finale, Why the Show Really Is Over and Not Knowing Abou
body:
Aug 19, 2026 4:00pm PT	
	

	
		‘Lucky’ Creators on Deciding Who Dies in the Finale, Why the Show Really Is Over and Not Knowing About Drew Starkey’s ‘Avid’ Fandom ‘Until We Killed Him’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Courtesy of Michael Becker/Apple TV
	

		
	
				

	SPOILER ALERT: This interview contains major spoilers from “All Good Things,” the finale of Apple TV’s “Lucky.”

	Luciana “Lucky” Armstrong (Anya Taylor-Joy) has just pulled off one last con on the most important person left in her life: her formerly incarcerated father, John (Timothy Olyphant).

	In the series finale of “Lucky,” the titular con artist pulls off a final scheme to win freedom for herself and her father from notorious gangster Wayne Whittaker (William Fichtner) and his dangerous underboss, Priscilla Masterson (Annette Bening) — who also happens to be Lucky’s disapproving mother-in-law. During a tense in-person meeting meant to hand over the $10 million she and her late husband, Cary (Drew Starkey), stole from Whittaker at John’s request, Lucky drops a bombshell: Whittaker had been secretly working with FBI agent Kershaw (Eric Lange) to track Cary, a betrayal that directly caused Cary’s fatal car crash in Episode 4. (Cary is also Whittaker’s biological son.)

	That revelation instantly jeopardizes Lucky’s tentative deal with FBI Agent Billie Rand (Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor). Billie had agreed to give Lucky and her father immunity, but only if Lucky could deliver the evidence needed to lock Whittaker up permanently. Listening in from a nearby water tower via a wire, Rand realizes Kershaw’s connection to the plot and holds him at gunpoint, sparking a fierce brawl between them. Meanwhile, on the ground below, Whittaker forces Lucky’s hand. Knowing that he needed a back-up plan, Whittaker’s men kidnapped John from his hotel room and beat him up to make Lucky reveal the crypto seed phrase needed to unlock the stolen $10 million.



	

									Michael Becker
	




	In the ensuing chaos, Whittaker tries to force Priscilla to execute Lucky right in front of John. But Priscilla turns her gun on Whittaker instead, gunning him down with three fatal shots in retaliation for Cary’s death. Priscilla ultimately allows Lucky and John to get off scot-free, believing that Lucky was the only other woman who truly loved her son.

	Though clear to keep the money, Lucky knows she can’t start fresh with stolen cash. Realizing her father would always risk her life for a con, she sets a trap: she sneakily reveals to John that the 12-word seed phrase is stored on a voice recorder hidden inside Cary’s childhood stuffed bear. By morning, John has vanished with the bear. But when he plays the tape, he finds a new message from Lucky — telling him he will never see her again, but that she orchestrated this to give him his ultimate freedom. Instead of keeping the fortune, Lucky hands the seed phrase and the $10 million over to Billie.

	Since wrapping production on “Lucky” just over a year ago, Jonathan Tropper and Cassie Pappas have both moved on to other Apple TV projects. Tropper is midway through production on the third season of “Your Friends & Neighbors,” which he describes as “pretty dark” but also “more romantic than past seasons.” Pappas, meanwhile, reveals that she is reteaming with her former “Silo” boss Graham Yost; in 2027, Yost will direct a feature written by Pappas, and the two are working together on a new (and currently unannounced) show titled “Lexicon.”


	But in a wide-ranging conversation with Variety, while breaking down the key creative changes they made in adapting Marissa Stapley’s novel “Lucky,” Tropper and Pappas addressed whether audiences have truly seen the last of the titular protagonist.
	

	
		Marissa Stapley gave you her blessing to take creative liberties with “Lucky.” In hindsight, what do you think was the hardest part of this adaptation for you to crack?	

	Jonathan Tropper: There was the density of story in the book that I knew we would not be able to fully carry over into a television show. So it was breaking down: What’s the essence of the story? What’s the essence of the characters? What to keep from the book, what we would have to jettison, and then what we would have to invent to make it work in seven episodes of television — I certainly hadn’t cracked that before Cassie came on, and we cracked it together over time.

	I had been able to write the pilot because that’s such a contained piece, but then figuring out what we were keeping, losing, and inventing beyond that was a struggle because we wanted to be really respectful to the themes and characters of the book. At the same time, it was like, “How do we convey this really complicated woman, and this really complicated father-daughter relationship that formed her? How do we convey that in a really taught thriller without having to tell all the backstory that’s in the book and without having to go into all of the flashbacks?” If we had 20 episodes, we could have done it, but how are we going to do this in seven or eight episodes? I think that was the biggest challenge.

	Cassie Pappas: The things that we invented or added that were not in the book were merely to help stakes and propulsion. So Agent Billie Rand didn’t exist in the book, but we knew we wanted literal heat at [Lucky’s] back chasing her down. I also like the idea of two women locked into [a dynamic where] neither one of them knows how to do anything else. Rand only knows how to hunt and find you, and Lucky only knows how to run.

	Tropper: We might’ve mentioned Pacino and De Niro in “Heat” a few times.

	Pappas: It’s this good guy/bad guy trope that we see, but I don’t know that I’ve seen two women locked in that dynamic. I was really interested in exploring, “How do women play that game differently?” because we’ve definitely seen men do it over and over. As we got into it, we realized, “So we’ve got a woman on the run, a female FBI agent chasing her, and a female mobster chasing her as well. But each one of those women also had a man above them — you’ve got Kershaw at the FBI above Rand, you’ve got John above Lucky, and you’ve got Wayne Whittaker above Priscilla.” That was a cool metaphor of wanting each one of them to shatter a glass ceiling of sorts. And by the end of the finale, each one of those women do.


	
		You chose to flesh out Lucky’s relationship with John, but you opted not to explore Lucky’s relationship with her mother, apart from a throwaway line in the show that suggests Lucky’s mother either died a long time ago or abandoned Lucky as a child. Why did you choose to focus on one relationship over the other?	

	Tropper: The father-daughter relationship was, to us, the heart of this show; the reason for doing the show was really to explore that. In this show, we wanted Lucky’s search to be her way out. It’s not about figuring out who her mother is; it’s about figuring out who she is. She’s never been given the opportunity to actually know who she is. So the search for a mother felt like it muddied the waters of what her throughline is, which was really a search for herself.

	Pappas: We both agreed that it made the stakes more clean if John is all she’s got, if she’s like, “This is all I’ve got in the world. He’s taught me how to live in this world the way he lives, and that’s all I know. I don’t know how to be vulnerable, I don’t know how to be empathetic, but I do know how to lift your wallet.” So I think there’s something interesting about her being able to be like, “My mom is dead, and that’s not even in the picture.”



	

									Michael Becker
	




	
		Anya Taylor-Joy was attached to star and executive produce this show long before you boarded the project as co-showrunners. What notes did she give during pre-production that ultimately influenced the trajectory of this story? Did she feel particularly strongly about any part of Lucky’s arc?	

	Pappas: She felt really strongly about Cary and their relationship. She felt very, very strongly that, when their parents went away to prison, Lucky and Cary got a taste of life outside of this criminal lifestyle. It was very important for her father to be the one that drags her back in, and that she didn’t want to be [involved in crime] when we meet her in the life. Because in a way, it creates a great underdog that you’re rooting for her to get out.

	Tropper: It’s pretty much a nonstop chase. She really wanted to make sure we were taking the time we needed for the character, and not just having her literally on the run for seven episodes without time to stop, explore different facets of what she’s doing, and slow down for the personal moments. [She wanted to explore] both the fear and the frustration of the con, and also the joy that she still feels against her better judgment when she pulls off a good con. She wanted to make sure that the chase was never at the expense of the character.


	
		How did you think about using those action sequences to reveal more about what is going on internally with Lucky?	

	Tropper: It’s always about where she is on the journey. So, for instance, in Episode 2, when she ends up with a grandmother and her two grandchildren in this very domestic setting, even as she’s conning them, you’re getting a sense of her seeing a life she never had — a mother figure, children, a dinner table, that kind of love and stability that she never had. So that’s what informs that whole episode. And then you go to Episode 4, which is this really high-octane car chase after she and Cary have found each other. But at the same time, while all that’s going on, where she’s really resolving her relationship with Carrie is during that car chase. So that whole car chase is the vehicle — no pun intended, or maybe pun intended, I don’t know — for her to resolve her situation with Cary literally at the last possible minute because then he dies. So I think it’s always story-formed. We just sit there and we think about: Where are we in the story? What is she running from or running to, and how do we express the character within that?


	
		Why did you choose to kill off Cary as early as you did in the show?	

	Pappas: I didn’t realize how avid Drew’s fans are until we killed him. I think that we thought about Cary as level one of the lessons she needed to learn, which was “I’m repeating a pattern that is similar to my dad, but I’m doing it with my husband.” So when we get him out of the picture, then she can look at who she really needs to get out from underneath is her father. It was really servicing that more than anything else, unless Tropper has a thing against “Outer Banks” fans.

	Tropper: No! I am shooting with an actor from “Outer Banks” today. [Writer’s note: Samantha Soule is guest-starring as a lawyer in an episode of Tropper’s “Your Friends & Neighbors” Season 3.] But it’s also the fact that we really always firmly believe that for Lucky to start the next part of her journey at the end of our show, she has to do it alone. She has to be freed from everything, and there have to be painful sacrifices for redemption because she’s not innocent, necessarily. We always knew that the last shot of Lucky was going to be Lucky alone stepping into a new life. So if she’s running off with her father or with Cary or with the money, she hasn’t fully extricated herself. We knew [Cary’s death] would be shocking, but we gave viewers the satisfaction of knowing that Cary had not intended to really leave her hanging.

	Pappas: I also think just narratively speaking, it always signals to the viewer that nobody’s safe.



	

									Michael Becker
	




	
		Lucky was born into this life of crime, but what intrigued you about the way she has learned to justify her actions? How does her moral compass bend over the course of the season as she wrestles with the consequences of her actions?	

	Pappas: I think that’s what Episode 5 is really about. She’s on the run [in Episodes] 2, 3, and 4, and the run keeps getting more propulsive into a car chase sequence where Cary dies. It’s after Cary’s death that she has to reckon with herself and the reality that her cons have consequences. It starts with that grandmother who was injured in the car crash, and she pretends that it’s her grandmother Ruth. But she has to look at that woman and remember, “Oh, that woman is injured because of me.” And then when the nurse asks, “What’s this woman’s medical history?,” she doesn’t have any answers. I think each one of these moments are like a blow to her.

	By the time that she’s sitting with that stranger at the bar in Episode 5, she goes into the routine of, “Here I go, I’m going to tell you this lie about how the reason I’m wearing these clothes is because the bellman got my bag wrong.” She stops and, for the very first time in her life, she chooses to be honest with someone. I think that’s truly where her moral compass starts to shift. The title of the episode is “Are We Bad People?,” because when she’s a kid, she asks her dad the same question. So if she’s been ruminating on that question her whole life, now as an adult, she gets to face herself and go, “I really hope I’m not a bad person. I don’t want to be a bad person. If I am, I don’t want to be.”

	Tropper: Her moral compass was bent before the show started; it’s been bent her whole life. So going into this, she has a skillset and she has a certain perspective of the role that’s been shaped largely by her father. From Episode 1, she’s doing things in a morally gray area, and that’s where she’s lived her whole life. It’s the unbending of her moral compass over the course of the season that gets her to where she needs to be.


	
		With any great crime thriller, you need a high dead body count — and two of the most satisfying deaths, Kershaw and Whittaker, happen in the finale. How did you settle on who died in the finale? Did you ever consider killing off, say, Priscilla or anyone else?	

	Tropper: We always knew that this is a show about three women who are pitted against each other. In a sense, there are three heroes and villains, and there was never a question that [the women] were not expendable, whereas everyone else around them was, depending on how the story worked.

	Pappas: I think pretty early days, Jonathan and I knew that Priscilla was going to shoot Wayne, and that it was going to be because of the love that was shared between her son and Lucky.



	

									Michael Becker
	



	
		And you always knew that Kershaw was a dirty FBI agent who was working with Whittaker the entire time?	

	Tropper: Yeah. Maybe not from day one, but certainly before we started writing scripts past the pilot, we were planning that, yes.
	
	
		Why do you think Priscilla chose to let Lucky and John go in the end?	

	Pappas: At this point, Priscilla has realized that Lucky is probably the only other person other than Priscilla that truly loved Cary. Deep down, there’s a part of Priscilla that’s still charmed by John. I know it’s not in the show, but we would always talk about [how] they probably had a pretty awesome affair before he started skimming from her.

	Tropper: There was a point where that was referenced more directly in the script, and we decided to couch it in a little more mystery. But there was a point where we actually referenced their sexual past. But beyond that, I’ve always felt — and there’s some dialogue in episode six that alludes to this — that Priscilla had a point in her life probably when she was around Lucky’s age where she wanted to get out too, and she couldn’t. There’s something in her that is vicariously living through Lucky’s escape.
	
		But the only way that Lucky was going to escape this life is by giving the money over to the FBI, right? Was there ever a version of this story where she kept the money or used it with her father?	

	Pappas: I think it’s pretty clear at the end where she’s given two choices. Her father is very clearly like, “We’ve got the money. What are you talking about? It’s in the bag. Let’s go.” She’s basically having to choose between those two options — what her dad wants and what she wants. What she wants is freedom, and the only way she’s going to be free is to get rid of this money.

	
		While there is still a tremendous amount of love between them, Lucky makes a clean break from John by the end of the show. What do you imagine their individual lives will look like after the screen cuts to black?	

	Pappas: I think John can’t help himself. He can’t help that he’s going to walk into a room and see a con and go back to his hustle. That’s just who he is. And for Lucky, I think she’s going to live a life that is on the straight and narrow, but free, and [she’ll] figure out who she really is without all the masks that she’s been wearing her whole life.

	Tropper: I would like to think that after a number of years of figuring herself out and learning to trust people and trust herself in certain situations, ultimately, she may want to have a child to give a child the life that she didn’t have.

	Pappas: In the [writers’] room, we did talk a lot about how criminals like this, whether it’s “Breaking Bad” or “Better Call Saul,” you walk into a room and you just see the world a certain way. That is how she sees the world, so I don’t think that she can unsee the way her father taught her to see the world. She’s probably always going to walk into a room and see a mark, but I believe that she can choose to not con that person. It’s like an alcoholic walking into a bar and not having a drink.


	
		“Lucky” was always billed as a miniseries, but in the current TV landscape, nothing in success ever really seems to be limited anymore. Did you ever toy around with a different ending? Did you ever think about extending the story beyond seven episodes?	

	Pappas: No, we wanted to make sure that we tied up all the loose ends and that it was a satisfying ending to a limited series.


	
		But Marissa is currently working on a sequel titled “No Such Thing As Lucky,” slated to come out in the fall of 2027. Would you ever adapt that book?	

	Tropper: We really poured our hearts into a one-and-done situation and we are both working on other things, but you never say never. Even from a purely business standpoint, I think the logistics of pulling this cast back together and doing this again would take a lot of doing. I think we would have to convince ourselves to a large extent that there would be a story worth telling, because there’s something so compelling about the resolution of these relationships in this one. And if the second one was just kind of like, “Lucky gets sucked back—”

	Pappas: “And goes on the run again!”

	Tropper: Yeah, I don’t think it would carry the same weight. I think it would feel very much like a business decision. So right now, I personally don’t see us doing that.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

title: French Soccer Star Kylian Mbappé Debuts New Golden Nike Cleats on Heels of World Cup Golden Boot Award Win
description:

	The World
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	The World Cup may be over but the merch and apparel rollout continues this month with the launch of a limited-edition pair of soccer cleats from French star and 2026 Golden Boot Award winner, Kylian Mbappé.

	The Nike Mercurial Superfly 11 reimagines the brand’s bestselling soccer cleats in a gold, white and mint colorway (matching the French national team’s 2026 away kit, which pays homage to France gifting the Statue of Liberty to the U.S. in 1884). The main upper uses Nike’s “FlyWeave Ultra” material, which offers a premium textured look with a golden shimmer. Nike’s Air Zoom cushioning and “ZoomX” foam offer comfort and responsiveness off the pitch.


		

						
			
	

					Nike
	
					
		

										NEW RELEASE						

					Nike Mercurial Superfly 11 Elite Kylian Mbappé		

		
	

	Mbappé’s “KM” initials and signature adorn a placard on the inner sole, which note that the cleats were “engineered to the exact specifications” of the soccer star. The words “Hungry for More” are seen on a mint green panel on the underfoot, further cementing the 27-year-old’s drive. 

	Nike has the Kylian Mbappé signature boot in men’s sizes 4 to 13, though units are selling out quickly online so we recommend picking them up online while they’re still available. You can see the full range of these low-top cleats at Nike.com.

	Mbappé has already been photographed wearing his new cleats, with the Real Madrid star sporting them on the pitch for the team’s 2026–27 La Liga season.



	

									Nike
	



	The golden colorway of this release is a fitting tribute to Mbappé, who won the Golden Boot Award at the recent World Cup as the tournament’s top goal scorer. The French forward scored 10 goals in this summer’s tournament and now has 22 World Cup goals in his career, making him the top World Cup goal scorer of all time. Argentinian star Lionel Messi sits second with 21 goals.


	Of course, Mbappé’s World Cup run came to an end in the semifinals when France lost 2-0 to eventual champion Spain. France then lost the third-place match by a score of 6-4 to England. 

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										ALSO AVAILABLE						

					Nike Academy Kylian Mbappé Soccer Ball		

		
	

	This is the 12th signature Nike Mercurial Kylian Mbappé Boot release. Nike also has an official Kylian Mbappé Academy soccer ball available for sale, in a metallic gold, “clear jade” and dark hazel colorway.

title: Academy Museum Fall Film Events Include ‘Marie Antoinette,’ ‘The Craft,’ ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ – Film News in Brief
description: The Academy Museum of Motion Pictures fall programming celebrates several anniversary milestones along with a focus on horror. There will be a 50th
body:
The Academy Museum of Motion Pictures fall programming celebrates several anniversary milestones along with a focus on horror. There will be a 50th anniversary screening of “Carrie” (1976) with Sissy Spacek, a 30th anniversary screening of “The Craft” (1996) with Rachel True and Robin Tunney and a 30th anniversary screening of “Get on the Bus” (1996). 

	There will also be a 20th anniversary screening of “Marie Antoinette” (2006) with Sofia Coppola. 
	

	“It’s hard to believe that Marie Antoinette was made 20 years ago,” Coppola said. “I am grateful that the film continues to have a life of its own and that new audiences are discovering their own ways into it through screenings like this one.” 


	John Carpenter will present the retrospective film series “John Carpenter: Prince of Darkness with John Carpenter.” 

	“I’m proud of these films and the worlds we created, and it’s gratifying to see they’ve found audiences and have taken on lives of their own,” Carpenter said. “It will be great to spend time together to look back at the work that has been such an important part of my life.”

	Other films programmed in conjunction with The Horror Show exhibit include a Monster Mash day with “Hotel Transylvania,” “Blade” and “Horror of Dracula.”

	There will also be a “Roberto Rossellini Prefers Real Life” screening series with Isabella Rossellini.

	“My father, Roberto Rossellini, had a deep curiosity about cinema, about people, and about the world that shaped my own curiosity and understanding of storytelling,” Isabella Rossellini said. “I’m delighted to share his films and to celebrate the legacy he left behind.”
	

	Museum members receive complimentary general admission for unlimited visits and priority admission. 
	
		Wednesday, August 19	

	Focus Features to Host Free Screening of ‘Finding Emily’ for People Named Emily

	If your name is Emily, you’re in luck. 

	Focus Features is hosting free previews of the romantic comedy “Finding Emily” for anybody named Emily and their friends this Sunday. The screening is only available in Los Angeles at AMC Century City and New York at AMC Empire 25 at 7 p.m..

	“Finding Emily” stars Angourie Rice and Spike Fearn as a musician who, after he dials a wrong number, embarks on a search for his dream girl with the help of a psychology student. 

	The film will release in theaters everywhere Aug. 28 and is from the team behind “Bridget Jones’s Diary” and “Love Actually.”
	
		Juan Gabriel’s “Bellas Artes” Concert Film Releasing Sept. 15 in U.S. Theaters	

	Juan Gabriel’s “Bellas Artes” concert film will release in U.S. theaters Sept. 15.

	“Juan Gabriel: Mi Primer Bellas Artes” is a newly re-edited and restored theatrical presentation of the singer-songwriter’s 1990 performance at Mexico City’s Palacio de Bellas Artes. It features a previously unseen introduction with rehearsal footage and personal archive materials.

	The six-time Grammy nominee is one of the all-time best-selling Latin music artists, with more than 100 million records sold over his four-decade career. A November 2025 screening of the concert at Mexico City’s Zócalo drew 170,000 attendees. The new theatrical edition will be released in Mexico, Spain and Latin America on Aug. 28, commemorating the 10th anniversary of Gabriel’s passing.

	The re-edit and restoration was led by María José Cuevas, the director and visual artist behind Netflix docuseries “Juan Gabriel: I Must, I Can, I Will,” in collaboration with production company MEZCLA. The film is produced by Sony Music Vision and distributed internationally by Cinemax Alternativo.

schema.headline: Academy Museum Fall Film Events Include ‘Marie Antoinette,’ ‘The Craft,’ ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ – Film News in Brief

title: Sandra Bullock Opens Up for the First Time on ALS Death of Partner Bryan Randall: ‘My Person Left A Lot Earlier Than the Body Left’
description:
Sandra Bullock is opening up about the death of her late partner Bryan Randall.

	The “Practical Magic 2” star made the rare remarks about her priva
body:
Sandra Bullock is opening up about the death of her late partner Bryan Randall.

	The “Practical Magic 2” star made the rare remarks about her private life during an appearance on the Smartless podcast hosted by Jason Bateman, Sean Hayes and Will Arnett.

	Randall, a photographer, battled ALS before dying on Aug. 5, 2023 at the age of 57. He and Bullock had been together eight years at the time of his death.


	Bullock said Randall asked her to keep his diagnosis a secret. “He asked me not to share. I know why he asked me not to,” Bullock said (via E! News.). “My sister [Gesine Bullock-Prado] was the only one who knew for a while.”
	

	She admitted that the secrecy “isolated me in the process.” 

	“My sister was the only one who knew for a while,” Bullock explained. “At first I go, ‘Oh, I can handle that. I can be quiet.’”

	However, caring for Randall and raising her two young kids during the Covid pandemic became “a trifecta that was pretty dark,” Bullock said.

	She eventually shared what was going on with friends Jennifer Aniston and Bateman’s wife, Amanda. “I think where he was in his journey, both physically and mentally, I started grieving Bryan four years before he passed,” Bullock said. “There was something that had shifted.”

	Bullock said Randall was sick for at least half of the eight years they were together. “My person left a lot earlier than the body left,” she said. “I don’t think I ever dealt with that until after he passed, because you’re just on this treadmill.”

	Bullock and Randall reportedly started dating in January 2015 after she hired him to photograph her son Louis’ fifth birthday party. They made their red-carpet debut 10 months later at the “Our Brand is Crisis” premiere in Los Angeles.
	

	“Bryan chose to keep his journey with ALS private and those of us who cared for him did our best to honor his request,” Randall’s family said in a statement following his passing. “We are immensely grateful to the tireless doctors who navigated the landscape of this illness with us and to the astounding nurses who became our roommates, often sacrificing their own families to be with ours. At this time we ask for privacy to grieve and to come to terms with the impossibility of saying goodbye to Bryan.”

schema.headline: Sandra Bullock Opens Up for the First Time on ALS Death of Partner Bryan Randall: ‘My Person Left A Lot Earlier Than the Body Left’

                              August 19, 2026
                            5:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            "Love After Lockup" star LaTisha Collier's pregnancy started with twins ... but she tells TMZ only one of the babies survived.
      
    
            LaTisha and husband Keith Collier tell us they found out they were expecting twins in early June ... but later learned one didn't make it. They say the other baby is doing well and is due in February -- on Keith's birthday.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The couple is hoping for a boy ... LaTisha already has daughters and says she'd love to have a biological son.
      

            LaTisha revealed her pregnancy on Instagram Tuesday -- her 40th birthday. She says the pregnancy has been "hell" so far ... with exhaustion, morning sickness and even an aversion to her beloved fried chicken.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            LaTisha also tells us the judge who sentenced her to 15 years knew she was pregnant ... because she told him herself.
      
    
            She admits pregnancy isn't a "get out of jail free card" ... but says she wanted the judge to be aware.
      
    
            As we previously reported ... LaTisha was released from prison earlier this month ... and she'll be out until a decision's made about her appeal -- after she was sentenced to 15 years behind bars for allegedly scamming clients of her financial firm.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The reality star was charged with felonies for forgery and identity theft ... but the identity theft charge was ultimately dropped.
      
    
            Despite the possibility of returning to prison, LaTisha and Keith say they're leaning on "fight and faith." She says she's complying with everything the court requires ... and won't do anything to jeopardize her freedom or being home for the birth.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            For now, LaTisha says she's focusing on the pregnancy ... and reviving her "Stiletto Wearing Felon" brand while she's out.
